Johnnie Walker is the blending house that reshaped how we look at, talk about, and drink whisky. We have published rankings like this before, but with new releases arriving at our door, it is time for an update.

As always, let us know in the comments which Johnnie Walker label is your favourite. Have I missed one? Would you rank them differently? Starting from worst to best, in last place we have…

## Johnnie Walker Red Label, 40%, [$25](https://compare.thewhiskeywash.com/search?searchTerm=johnnie%20walker%20red%20label&sortOrder=1&sortField=price_gbp&sortKey=%7B%22label%22%3A%22Sort%3A%20Lowest%20price%22%2C%22value%22%3A%22price_gbp%22%7D&filters=%7B%22price_range%22%3A%5B0%2C383200%5D%2C%22ui_my_country_id%22%3A234%2C%22ui_us_state_id%22%3Anull%2C%22country_id%22%3A0%2C%22my_location_id%22%3A234%2C%22retail%22%3Atrue%2C%22auction%22%3Afalse%2C%22excludes%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22priceRangeScale%22%3A%5B0%2C1000%5D%2C%22onlyShippable%22%3Afalse%2C%22fullSizeOnly%22%3Atrue%2C%22minPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22maxPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22trigger_price%22%3Anull%2C%22currency_id%22%3A1%7D&secondaryFilters=%7B%22abv%22%3Anull%2C%22age%22%3Anull%2C%22bottleSize%22%3Anull%2C%22bottledYear%22%3Anull%2C%22bottler%22%3Anull%2C%22distillery%22%3Anull%2C%22caskNumber%22%3Anull%2C%22vintage%22%3Anull%7D)

No surprises here. Red Label is not trying to be bad; it is simply made to hit a very accessible price point.

As a result, it contains very young whiskies that do not offer the depth or character found elsewhere in the Johnnie Walker range.

It can be sipped neat, but it is really a mixer. Serve it tall with ginger beer, ice, and lime for a tasty long drink.

## Johnnie Walker Gold Label Reserve, 40%, [$45](https://compare.thewhiskeywash.com/search?searchTerm=johnnie%20walker%20gold%20label&sortOrder=1&sortField=price_gbp&sortKey=%7B%22label%22%3A%22Sort%3A%20Lowest%20price%22%2C%22value%22%3A%22price_gbp%22%7D&filters=%7B%22price_range%22%3A%5B0%2C383200%5D%2C%22ui_my_country_id%22%3A234%2C%22ui_us_state_id%22%3Anull%2C%22country_id%22%3A0%2C%22my_location_id%22%3A234%2C%22retail%22%3Atrue%2C%22auction%22%3Afalse%2C%22excludes%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22priceRangeScale%22%3A%5B0%2C1000%5D%2C%22onlyShippable%22%3Afalse%2C%22fullSizeOnly%22%3Atrue%2C%22minPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22maxPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22trigger_price%22%3Anull%2C%22currency_id%22%3A1%7D&secondaryFilters=%7B%22abv%22%3Anull%2C%22age%22%3Anull%2C%22bottleSize%22%3Anull%2C%22bottledYear%22%3Anull%2C%22bottler%22%3Anull%2C%22distillery%22%3Anull%2C%22caskNumber%22%3Anull%2C%22vintage%22%3Anull%7D)

Gold Label has always been a paradox. It promises luxury but consistently falls short. The nose is sweet and fruity, which is lovely, but the palate lacks a defining standout character, especially when compared with Black Label or Green Label.

Years ago, when Gold Label carried an 18-year age statement, it was outrageously good. You could taste the Royal Lochnagar and Clynelish influence, giving it that rich, waxy profile. Today it lives in the shadow of that era, albeit in a flashy gold bottle.

## Johnnie Walker Double Black, 40%, [$33](https://compare.thewhiskeywash.com/search?searchTerm=johnnie%20walker%20double%20black&sortOrder=1&sortField=price_gbp&sortKey=%7B%22label%22%3A%22Sort%3A%20Lowest%20price%22%2C%22value%22%3A%22price_gbp%22%7D&filters=%7B%22price_range%22%3A%5B0%2C383200%5D%2C%22ui_my_country_id%22%3A234%2C%22ui_us_state_id%22%3Anull%2C%22country_id%22%3A0%2C%22my_location_id%22%3A234%2C%22retail%22%3Atrue%2C%22auction%22%3Afalse%2C%22excludes%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22priceRangeScale%22%3A%5B0%2C1000%5D%2C%22onlyShippable%22%3Afalse%2C%22fullSizeOnly%22%3Atrue%2C%22minPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22maxPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22trigger_price%22%3Anull%2C%22currency_id%22%3A1%7D&secondaryFilters=%7B%22abv%22%3Anull%2C%22age%22%3Anull%2C%22bottleSize%22%3Anull%2C%22bottledYear%22%3Anull%2C%22bottler%22%3Anull%2C%22distillery%22%3Anull%2C%22caskNumber%22%3Anull%2C%22vintage%22%3Anull%7D)

This is another bottle that feels slightly out of place. On paper, it should be brilliant – Black Label with more smoky whiskies. Great. The issue is that there is no age statement, the ABV is not higher, and it contains more grain whisky.

The extra smoke ends up balanced rather than amplified. Balance is not a bad thing, but when you call something Double Black and promise more smoke, that is what drinkers expect. It could be excellent, genuinely, but it never quite gets there for me.

## Johnnie Walker Black Ruby, 40%, [$33](https://compare.thewhiskeywash.com/search?searchTerm=johnnie%20walker%20black%20ruby&sortOrder=1&sortField=price_gbp&sortKey=%7B%22label%22%3A%22Sort%3A%20Lowest%20price%22%2C%22value%22%3A%22price_gbp%22%7D&filters=%7B%22price_range%22%3A%5B0%2C383200%5D%2C%22ui_my_country_id%22%3A236%2C%22ui_us_state_id%22%3A250%2C%22country_id%22%3A0%2C%22my_location_id%22%3A250%2C%22retail%22%3Atrue%2C%22auction%22%3Afalse%2C%22excludes%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22priceRangeScale%22%3A%5B0%2C1000%5D%2C%22onlyShippable%22%3Afalse%2C%22fullSizeOnly%22%3Atrue%2C%22minPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22maxPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22trigger_price%22%3Anull%2C%22currency_id%22%3A1%7D&secondaryFilters=%7B%22abv%22%3Anull%2C%22age%22%3Anull%2C%22bottleSize%22%3Anull%2C%22bottledYear%22%3Anull%2C%22bottler%22%3Anull%2C%22distillery%22%3Anull%2C%22caskNumber%22%3Anull%2C%22vintage%22%3Anull%7D)

A new addition to the range, Black Ruby mirrors the blueprint of Black Label but without the age statement. It features additional maturation in Oloroso sherry, Pedro Ximénez sherry, and red wine seasoned barrels. The latter is particularly interesting, as it has only appeared in experimental Johnnie Walker releases.

It is genuinely tasty. With time in the glass it shows a red-fruit sweetness with a gentle thread of smoke. It is good, but the regular Black Label still outshines it.

## Johnnie Walker Blue Label, 40%, [$190](https://compare.thewhiskeywash.com/search?searchTerm=johnnie%20walker%20blue%20label&sortOrder=1&sortField=price_gbp&sortKey=%7B%22label%22%3A%22Sort%3A%20Lowest%20price%22%2C%22value%22%3A%22price_gbp%22%7D&filters=%7B%22price_range%22%3A%5B0%2C383200%5D%2C%22ui_my_country_id%22%3A236%2C%22ui_us_state_id%22%3A250%2C%22country_id%22%3A0%2C%22my_location_id%22%3A250%2C%22retail%22%3Atrue%2C%22auction%22%3Afalse%2C%22excludes%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22priceRangeScale%22%3A%5B0%2C1000%5D%2C%22onlyShippable%22%3Afalse%2C%22fullSizeOnly%22%3Atrue%2C%22minPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22maxPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22trigger_price%22%3Anull%2C%22currency_id%22%3A1%7D&secondaryFilters=%7B%22abv%22%3Anull%2C%22age%22%3Anull%2C%22bottleSize%22%3Anull%2C%22bottledYear%22%3Anull%2C%22bottler%22%3Anull%2C%22distillery%22%3Anull%2C%22caskNumber%22%3Anull%2C%22vintage%22%3Anull%7D)

Blue Label is the most expensive and arguably the most famous bottle here. Do I like it? Yes, I do. It is elegant, balanced, and very drinkable. Is it worth the money? No, not really.

If I handed $190 over to you and told you to buy a bottle of whisky, I doubt you’d walk out of the shop with this in your hands.

It is gentle, sweet, lightly smoky, and impeccably made, but for almost $200 you can find bottles with far more drama and complexity.

## Johnnie Walker 18 Year Old, 40%, [$77](https://compare.thewhiskeywash.com/search?searchTerm=johnnie%20walker%2018%20year%20old&sortOrder=1&sortField=price_gbp&sortKey=%7B%22label%22%3A%22Sort%3A%20Lowest%20price%22%2C%22value%22%3A%22price_gbp%22%7D&filters=%7B%22price_range%22%3A%5B0%2C383200%5D%2C%22ui_my_country_id%22%3A236%2C%22ui_us_state_id%22%3A250%2C%22country_id%22%3A0%2C%22my_location_id%22%3A250%2C%22retail%22%3Atrue%2C%22auction%22%3Afalse%2C%22excludes%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22priceRangeScale%22%3A%5B0%2C1000%5D%2C%22onlyShippable%22%3Afalse%2C%22fullSizeOnly%22%3Atrue%2C%22minPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22maxPrice%22%3Atrue%2C%22trigger_price%22%3Anull%2C%22currency_id%22%3A1%7D&secondaryFilters=%7B%22abv%22%3Anull%2C%22age%22%3Anull%2C%22bottleSize%22%3Anull%2C%22bottledYear%22%3Anull%2C%22bottler%22%3Anull%2C%22distillery%22%3Anull%2C%22caskNumber%22%3Anull%2C%22vintage%22%3Anull%7D)

This is a better bottle than Blue Label. It costs less and offers more. Driven by highland single malts, it shows toffee, gentle smoke, grassiness, warm caramel, and a subtle flash of old grain whisky. It feels luxurious without trying too hard.

I would happily choose this over many far older bottles on the market. It is delicious and relatively affordable for what it delivers.

Johnnie Walker is the world’s best-selling scotch whisky. Its bottles are arranged in clear levels, from everyday blends to luxury drams.

Many drinkers ask what those levels are and how they compare. The answer is simple. Each label is designed to match a different taste, price point, and occasion.

## Signup now to make sure you don't miss out on the latest whiskey news and deals.

## Signup now to make sure you don't miss out on the latest whiskey news and deals.

This guide walks you through the range, from Red Label at the base to Blue Label at the top.

## Understanding the Johnnie Walker Levels

When people talk about the “levels” of Johnnie Walker, they usually mean price, flavor, and maturity. The range moves in a straight line from lighter, younger whiskies to older, more complex blends.

Not every bottle carries an age statement. Some are built for smoothness and balance rather than age. What matters is how the whisky is blended. Red Label is young and bold. Black Label is older and more refined. Green and Gold bring extra depth. The 18 Year Old and Blue Label sit at the top as premium choices.

The goal is simple. Johnnie Walker makes a whisky for every taste and every occasion, whether you want a highball with friends or a luxury dram to savor.

## Level 1: Johnnie Walker Red Label

Red Label is the entry point into the Johnnie Walker range. It is a no-age-statement blend made from grain and malt whiskies aged at least three years. The focus is on vibrancy rather than maturity.

The flavor is light, with crisp apple, citrus, and a touch of spice. A faint smokiness appears on the finish, but this is a whisky built for mixing rather than sipping neat, and does not offer the complexity of the high-level bottlings.

In the U.S., a bottle usually costs $20 – $30. In the UK, expect to pay about £20.

Red Label is best suited for casual drinkers who want something simple and affordable. It can be used well in long drinks, particularly the Johnnie & Ginger, where whisky is mixed with ginger ale and a squeeze of lime.

## Level 2: Johnnie Walker Black Label

Black Label is the first step up in the range. Every whisky in the blend is aged for at least 12 years, bringing more depth and balance than Red Label. Around 40 different malts and grains are used, including smoky Islay whisky and sweet Speyside whisky.

The flavor is smooth and complex. You get dried fruit, vanilla, and toffee at the start, followed by gentle spice and a clean thread of smoke. The finish is medium length, with cocoa and oak.

In the U.S., it sells for about $30–$35. In the UK, it is usually £25–£30.

Black Label works for almost anyone. New drinkers get a balanced introduction to Scotch, and experienced drinkers respect its consistency. It can be sipped neat, but it also makes a strong Rob Roy or a simple highball with soda water or ginger ale.

## Level 3: Johnnie Walker Double Black

Double Black was created as a bolder version of Black Label. It does not carry an age statement, but it uses more smoky malts from the west coast and Islay, as well as whiskies matured in deeply charred oak casks.

The flavor is fuller and smokier than Black Label. Expect bonfire smoke, charred wood, and dark spice balanced by sweet vanilla. The finish is dry and slightly ashy, with lingering peat.

In the U.S., a bottle is usually $40–$45. In the UK, it is around £35.

Double Black is best for drinkers who enjoy smoke but want a smooth blend rather than a heavy Islay single malt. It is good neat or with ice, but also works in a Penicillin, where the smoke pairs with honey, ginger, and lemon. A simple smoky highball with soda water is another easy option.

## Level 4: Johnnie Walker Green Label

Green Label is different from the rest of the range. It is a blended malt, meaning it contains only single malts and no grain whisky. Every whisky in the blend is aged at least 15 years. Key malts include Talisker, Caol Ila, Cragganmore, and Linkwood.

The flavor is layered and balanced. You get citrus and orchard fruits alongside smoke, oak, and herbs. A gentle peppery spice carries through to the finish, which lingers with soft smoke and malt sweetness.

In the U.S., Green Label usually costs $60–$75. In the UK, it is around £45–£50.

This whisky suits drinkers who want more depth than standard blends but not the intensity of cask-strength single malts. It is best enjoyed neat or with a splash of water. For a cocktail, a Rob Roy highlights its complex character without hiding its smoky edge.

## Level 5: Johnnie Walker Gold Label Reserve

Gold Label Reserve is a no-age-statement blend created for smoothness and celebration. The lead malt is Clynelish, known for its waxy and honeyed style, which gives the whisky a rich and creamy base.

The flavor is sweet and mellow. Expect honey, vanilla, and ripe stone fruits, with just a whisper of smoke on the finish. It is less smoky and more indulgent than Black or Double Black.

In the U.S., it typically sells for $60-$80. In the UK, it is about £50-£55.

Gold Label Reserve is designed for those who enjoy sweeter, softer whiskies. It is a crowd-pleaser at parties and works well in cocktails. A Whisky Sour with Gold Label is rich and honeyed. For something simpler, try it with soda water and an orange slice for a refreshing highball.

## Level 6: Johnnie Walker 18 Year Old (Formerly Platinum Label)

The 18 Year Old is one of the most refined whiskies in the Johnnie Walker range. Every component has been matured for at least 18 years, giving it a rich and polished character. The blend draws heavily on Speyside malts, balanced with a touch of smoke from Islay.

The flavor is elegant and smooth. Up front, you get honey, dried fruit, and vanilla. Mid-palate brings citrus, warm spice, and soft oak. A gentle smoke lingers on the finish, with notes of toffee and dark chocolate.

In the U.S., it usually costs $70–$90. In the UK, it is around £65–£75.

This whisky suits drinkers who want maturity and depth without the intensity of cask-strength single malts. It is a strong value in the premium category and is best enjoyed neat or with a splash of water. For a subtle twist, it can also make a very smooth Old Fashioned.

## Level 7: Johnnie Walker Blue Label

Blue Label is the flagship of the Johnnie Walker range. It does not carry an age statement, but it is blended from rare and often very old casks drawn from across Scotland. Only a small fraction of the whiskies in Johnnie Walker’s reserves are considered good enough to make it into Blue Label.

The flavor is luxurious and layered. Hazelnut, dark chocolate, and dried fruit lead the palate, followed by spice and a deep, silky smoke. The finish is long and warming, with a balance of sweetness and soft oak.

In the U.S., a bottle costs $180–$250. In the UK, it usually sells for £130–£180.

Blue Label is designed for special occasions. It is smooth enough for almost anyone to enjoy, yet complex enough for seasoned whisky drinkers to appreciate. The brand recommends drinking it neat, with a glass of chilled water on the side to cleanse the palate.

## Beyond the Johnnie Walker Core Range

Johnnie Walker also produces a number of limited editions and luxury bottlings. These sit above Blue Label in prestige and often include rare stocks from closed distilleries. Examples include King George V, John Walker & Sons Odyssey, and Ghost & Rare editions. They are not part of the everyday levels but are released in small batches for collectors and special occasions.

## How the Levels of Johnnie Walker Stack Up

The Johnnie Walker levels move in a clear line. Red Label is bold and simple, designed for mixing. Black Label adds maturity and balance. Double Black increases the smoke. Green Label brings complexity as a blended malt. Gold Label Reserve is smooth and celebratory. The 18 Year Old delivers refinement and value. Blue Label sits at the top as a symbol of luxury.

Each bottle is crafted for a purpose. Whether you are new to scotch or a long-time enthusiast, there is a Johnnie Walker that fits your taste and your budget.

So, what is your favorite Johnnie Walker whisky? Let us know in the comments.

Chivas Regal is one of the bestselling blended Scotch whisky brands in the world. More importantly it was one of the first whiskies I ever tried. I wanted to do a proper review of the seven main Chivas Regal whiskies to see what they were like in general and how they compared with each other. Here’s what I found.

## 1. Chivas Regal 12 Year Old

### About

- 40%ABV
- Price: $34.99 approx. for 750ml

This whisky is a blend of 40 plus malt and grain whiskies – mostly grain whiskies and mostly from the Speyside region of Scotland – that have been matured for at least 12 years.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Amber, gold

Nose: Apple, vanilla, toffee, honey, cereal, fruit, caramel

Taste: Honey, apples, caramel, fruit, grain, floral, vanilla

Finish: Short: Bitter, apple, grain, spice, fruit

Score – 72 / 100

### Summary

Chivas Regal 12 is a sweet and smooth whisky that’s very easy to drink and difficult not to like. This makes it perfect for a wider audience and with whiskies like this it’s no wonder that Chivas Regal is one of the bestselling blended Scotch whisky brands in the world.

Of course, being a blended whisky, it has less flavors than your average single malt so you may find it too plain or boring in comparison. On the other hand, it does have enough flavors to make it better than other blends.

It’s also a decent quality whisky for a relatively low price.

## 2. Chivas Mizunara

### About

- 40% ABV
- Price: $49.99 approx. for 750ml

Chivas Mizunara is Chivas Regal 12, parts of which are finished in Mizunara casks.

Mizunara is a rare and expensive type of oak from the northern Japanese island of Hokkaido, that’s sometimes used in Japanese distilling to mature malts. Mizunara is a more humid and porous wood which means that casks made from it will have a greater influence on the flavor of the whisky.

Chivas doesn’t say how much of the whisky is finished in Mizunara casks or for how long but taking into account the fact that Mizunara is as mentioned, rare and expensive, but the price of a bottle is only around $50, I would estimate the answers are ‘not much’ and ‘not too long’ respectively.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Amber, gold

Nose: Vanilla, honey, caramel, orange, apples, pears, toffee, cinnamon, herbs, cereal

Taste: Vanilla, oak, pears, honey, caramel, apples, oranges, pepper, cereal, clove

Finish: Short – medium: Oak, apples, pepper, honey, toffee, vanilla. Starts sweet but ends bitter

Score – 70 / 100

### Summary

There was some influence from the Mizunara casks and the sweet caramel and vanilla flavors of the 12 were somewhat enhanced by mild exotic herbal notes and a bit of spice coming from the Mizunara casks, but it’s minimal and you really have to pay attention, especially on the nose, if you want to pick them up.

It may therefore be a slight improvement on the 12, but the minimal amount means that for me, this is only a whisky to try occasionally – to see if I get a better result.

## 3. Chivas Extra 13 Sherry Cask

### About

- 40%ABV
- Price: $41.99 approx. for 750ml

This is classic Chivas Regal that’s been aged for at least 13 years, parts of it in ex-Oloroso sherry casks so as to magnify the sweet and rich notes of the whisky.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Deep amber, gold

Nose: Caramel, chocolate, sherry, pears, apples, toffee, vanilla, oak

Taste: Vanilla, caramel, sherry, fruit, oak, grain, toffee

Finish: Short – Medium: Spices, oak, caramel

Score – 74 / 100

### Summary

Like the 12, the Chivas Extra 13 is sweet, smooth and easy to drink. The extra year doesn’t give this whisky that many more flavors, so it still has less flavors than your average single malt but this time, there’s definitely a sherry character and sweetness to this whisky that comes from the cask.

If you like sherry and you like Chivas, then it’s worth trying out this expression since it’s not that much more expensive than the 12.

### About

- 40% ABV
- Price: $44.24 approx. for 700ml

This Chivas blend is aged for at least 15 years, parts of which are finished in casks that previously held cognac. Hence the XV as opposed to 15, which is a nod to the cognac system that tends to use letters such as XO (Extra Old) and VS (Very Special) rather than age statements.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Light amber

Nose: Honey, vanilla, cinnamon, oak, raisins, caramel, apples, pear, cognac

Taste: Caramel, toffee, vanilla, pears, oak, cinnamon, apples, honey, raisins

Finish: Medium – long: Spicy, vanilla, fruity, sweet, bitter

Score – 76 / 100

### Summary

This is another Chivas whisky that’s sweet, smooth and easy to drink and while it’s definitely more complex and fruity than the 12, we’re still not into single malt territory yet.

As for the effect of the cognac cask on the whisky, it was noticeable but limited, somewhat enhancing the fruity flavors in the Chivas blend.

## 5. Chivas Regal 18 Year Old

### About

- 40% ABV
- Price: $82.99 approx. for 750ml

This whisky is aged for at least 18 years and has, Chivas claims, 85 flavor notes in every drop! Spoiler alert – it doesn’t. I couldn’t pick out all 85 flavors over many drops let alone in one.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Amber

Nose: Caramel, sherry, malt, toffee, vanilla, honey, dried fruits, oak, peat

Taste: Vanilla, honey, smoke, caramel, malt, oak, orange, sherry, chocolate

Finish: Short to medium: Smoke, grain, oak

Score – 80 / 100

### Summary

Chivas Regal 18 is a good progression on the 12. It has many of the same elements (sweet, smooth and easy to drink) but the six extra years give it a much-needed maturity, which makes it pretty complex for a blended whisky.

The only problem is that it’s not a good enough progression to justify it being twice the price, for which you could buy something that would make the Chivas Regal 18 flavorless by comparison.

## 6. Chivas Regal 25 Years

### About

- 40% ABV
- Price: $362.99 approx. for 750ml

This whisky is aged for at least 25 years and costs over $350. Need I say more.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Deep gold

Nose: Caramel, vanilla, almonds, marzipan, chocolate, honey, orange, raisins

Taste: Vanilla, oak, oranges, chocolate, ginger, smoky, marmalade, caramel

Finish: Medium – long: Chocolate, smoke, oak

Score – 85 / 100

### Summary

The Chivas Regal 25 Year Old is good. Very good. It’s only 40%ABV but it’s full of flavors and they’re delicious. It has a good weight on the palate with a soft, rich, and creamy mouthfeel.

And it’s smooth. It’s not the smoothest whisky in the world but it’s very, very smooth.

It’s also expensive. It’s not the most expensive whisky in the world but it’s very, very expensive.

## 7. Chivas Regal Ultis

### About

- 66.85% ABV
- Price: $189.99 approx. for 750ml

Chivas Regal Ultis is a departure from the traditional Chivas blend because it only contains malt whiskies. It’s blended from five of the main single malts Chivas uses to create their whiskies: Allt A’Bhainne, Braeval, Longmorn, Strathisla and Tormore.

Of course, being a blended whisky, it has less flavors than your average single malt so you may find it too plain or boring in comparison. On the other hand, it does have enough flavors to make it better than other blends.

It’s also a decent quality whisky for a relatively low price.

## 2. Chivas Mizunara

### About

- 40% ABV
- Price: $49.99 approx. for 750ml

Chivas Mizunara is Chivas Regal 12, parts of which are finished in Mizunara casks.

Mizunara is a rare and expensive type of oak from the northern Japanese island of Hokkaido, that’s sometimes used in Japanese distilling to mature malts. Mizunara is a more humid and porous wood which means that casks made from it will have a greater influence on the flavor of the whisky.

Chivas doesn’t say how much of the whisky is finished in Mizunara casks or for how long but taking into account the fact that Mizunara is as mentioned, rare and expensive, but the price of a bottle is only around $50, I would estimate the answers are ‘not much’ and ‘not too long’ respectively.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Amber, gold

Nose: Vanilla, honey, caramel, orange, apples, pears, toffee, cinnamon, herbs, cereal

Taste: Vanilla, oak, pears, honey, caramel, apples, oranges, pepper, cereal, clove

Finish: Short – medium: Oak, apples, pepper, honey, toffee, vanilla. Starts sweet but ends bitter

Score – 70 / 100

### Summary

There was some influence from the Mizunara casks and the sweet caramel and vanilla flavors of the 12 were somewhat enhanced by mild exotic herbal notes and a bit of spice coming from the Mizunara casks, but it’s minimal and you really have to pay attention, especially on the nose, if you want to pick them up.

It may therefore be a slight improvement on the 12, but the minimal amount means that for me, this is only a whisky to try occasionally – to see if I get a better result.

## 3. Chivas Extra 13 Sherry Cask

### About

- 40%ABV
- Price: $41.99 approx. for 750ml

This is classic Chivas Regal that’s been aged for at least 13 years, parts of it in ex-Oloroso sherry casks so as to magnify the sweet and rich notes of the whisky.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Deep amber, gold

Nose: Caramel, chocolate, sherry, pears, apples, toffee, vanilla, oak

Taste: Vanilla, caramel, sherry, fruit, oak, grain, toffee

Finish: Short – Medium: Spices, oak, caramel

Score – 74 / 100

### Summary

Like the 12, the Chivas Extra 13 is sweet, smooth and easy to drink. The extra year doesn’t give this whisky that many more flavors, so it still has less flavors than your average single malt but this time, there’s definitely a sherry character and sweetness to this whisky that comes from the cask.

If you like sherry and you like Chivas, then it’s worth trying out this expression since it’s not that much more expensive than the 12.

### About

- 40% ABV
- Price: $44.24 approx. for 700ml

This Chivas blend is aged for at least 15 years, parts of which are finished in casks that previously held cognac. Hence the XV as opposed to 15, which is a nod to the cognac system that tends to use letters such as XO (Extra Old) and VS (Very Special) rather than age statements.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Light amber

Nose: Honey, vanilla, cinnamon, oak, raisins, caramel, apples, pear, cognac

Taste: Caramel, toffee, vanilla, pears, oak, cinnamon, apples, honey, raisins

Finish: Medium – long: Spicy, vanilla, fruity, sweet, bitter

Score – 76 / 100

### Summary

This is another Chivas whisky that’s sweet, smooth and easy to drink and while it’s definitely more complex and fruity than the 12, we’re still not into single malt territory yet.

As for the effect of the cognac cask on the whisky, it was noticeable but limited, somewhat enhancing the fruity flavors in the Chivas blend.

## 5. Chivas Regal 18 Year Old

### About

- 40% ABV
- Price: $82.99 approx. for 750ml

This whisky is aged for at least 18 years and has, Chivas claims, 85 flavor notes in every drop! Spoiler alert – it doesn’t. I couldn’t pick out all 85 flavors over many drops let alone in one.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Amber

Nose: Caramel, sherry, malt, toffee, vanilla, honey, dried fruits, oak, peat

Taste: Vanilla, honey, smoke, caramel, malt, oak, orange, sherry, chocolate

Finish: Short to medium: Smoke, grain, oak

Score – 80 / 100

### Summary

Chivas Regal 18 is a good progression on the 12. It has many of the same elements (sweet, smooth and easy to drink) but the six extra years give it a much-needed maturity, which makes it pretty complex for a blended whisky.

The only problem is that it’s not a good enough progression to justify it being twice the price, for which you could buy something that would make the Chivas Regal 18 flavorless by comparison.

## 6. Chivas Regal 25 Years

### About

- 40% ABV
- Price: $362.99 approx. for 750ml

This whisky is aged for at least 25 years and costs over $350. Need I say more.

### Tasting Notes

Color: Deep gold

Nose: Caramel, vanilla, almonds, marzipan, chocolate, honey, orange, raisins

Taste: Vanilla, oak, oranges, chocolate, ginger, smoky, marmalade, caramel

Finish: Medium – long: Chocolate, smoke, oak

Score – 85 / 100

### Summary

The Chivas Regal 25 Year Old is good. Very good. It’s only 40%ABV but it’s full of flavors and they’re delicious. It has a good weight on the palate with a soft, rich, and creamy mouthfeel.

And it’s smooth. It’s not the smoothest whisky in the world but it’s very, very smooth.

It’s also expensive. It’s not the most expensive whisky in the world but it’s very, very expensive.

## 7. Chivas Regal Ultis

### About

- 66.85% ABV
- Price: $189.99 approx. for 750ml

Chivas Regal Ultis is a departure from the traditional Chivas blend because it only contains malt whiskies. It’s blended from five of the main single malts Chivas uses to create their whiskies: Allt A’Bhainne, Braeval, Longmorn, Strathisla and Tormore.
